findings.title: Settings-handler falls back per row instead of per slot, so a workflow row hides all assistant-scoped selections
findings.problem: The handler reads the workflow-scoped row and consults the assistant-scoped one only when the workflow row is entirely absent, then scans that single row for the requested credential type. The service-level resolver added in the same change merges the two scopes per slot, and that is what the router, the panel and _apply_marketplace_tool_mappings use.
findings.impact: Two resolution paths disagree inside the same run: a slot selected only at assistant scope resolves to the author's base config (or a project integration) whenever any workflow row exists, while the panel shows the merged value. Wrong credential used, invisible from the UI. Violates AC12.
findings.recommendation: Build the same merged view in the handler (overlay the workflow row on the assistant row per slot, or reuse get_effective_tools_config), and add a test for 'workflow row exists but lacks the requested slot'.

findings.title: A slot cannot be cleared inside a workflow — 'None' re-inherits the assistant-scoped integration
findings.problem: An empty integration_id means 'remove the slot entry'. At assistant scope removal means 'fall back to base config'; at workflow scope it means 'inherit from the assistant scope', because the effective read re-adds every missing slot. There is no way to express an explicit workflow-level opt-out, and the frontend cannot send one.
findings.impact: A user cannot stop using their personal credential inside a single workflow: the reset is silently undone, the panel redisplays the old value after a success toast, and the two runtime paths disagree about the result.
findings.recommendation: Product decision required: either persist an explicit empty-integration tombstone in the workflow row (honoured as an override to base config by both resolvers), or state that clearing is not supported at workflow scope and disable it in the UI. Cover the chosen behaviour with a service test and a component test.

findings.title: Saving from the workflow panel snapshots inherited slots into the workflow row, freezing inheritance
findings.problem: The panel is seeded from the effective config and posts every displayed slot, so untouched slots whose value came from the assistant scope are written into the workflow row as overrides.
findings.impact: The inheritance the backend promises never happens after the first workflow-scoped save: later assistant-page changes (including rotating or deleting an integration) stop reaching that workflow, and nothing in the UI shows the slot is pinned.
findings.recommendation: Send only slots the user actually changed while a workflow scope is active (track dirty keys), or have the backend store only entries that differ from the effective assistant-scoped value. Add a test asserting one changed slot does not persist the inherited ones.

findings.title: Checkbox default is computed from the orchestrator but drives sub-assistant saves
findings.problem: applyToAssistant is initialised from the parent assistant's has_assistant_scope_selection and then passed to every sub-assistant save, although each sub-assistant has its own pair of scopes and its own flag (which UserMapping already fetches and discards).
findings.impact: A sub-assistant selection the user deliberately confined to one workflow can be promoted to assistant scope — reaching chat — and its workflow row deleted, without the user asking for it; the mirror case silently confines a sub-assistant's first-ever selection to one workflow.
findings.recommendation: Track the default per saved entity (use each sub-assistant's own flag), or render the scope control per Save block. Add a mixed parent/sub-assistant test.

findings.title: Checkbox state is never loaded when only sub-assistants have mappable slots
findings.problem: fetchUserMappingSettings — the only place that sets applyToAssistant from the backend — runs only when hasOrchestratorMapping is true, but the section and the checkbox render whenever sub-assistants have mappings.
findings.impact: For orchestrator-composed assistants the checkbox always shows its useState(false) default, so the documented pre-tick never applies and a first-ever selection is silently confined to one workflow.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the default from whichever mappings were actually loaded, or hide the checkbox when the orchestrator has no slots. Add a render test for the sub-assistants-only shape.

findings.title: has_assistant_scope_selection reports row existence, not an actual selection
findings.problem: The flag is `assistant_mapping is not None`, and the GET branch sets it to True whenever a row exists. A row whose tools_config is empty (the user cleared every slot) still reports True.
findings.impact: The checkbox default is wrong for exactly the case the flag exists to serve: a user with an empty leftover row gets the box unticked and their next selection is confined to one workflow.
findings.recommendation: Return `bool(assistant_mapping and assistant_mapping.tools_config)` and mirror it in the GET branch; add a service test for the empty-row case.

findings.title: Migration downgrade silently and irreversibly deletes every workflow-scoped selection
findings.problem: downgrade() runs an unconditional DELETE of all workflow-scoped rows before recreating the two-column constraint, and the column is dropped in the same step, so a re-upgrade cannot restore them. The predicate also misses any NULL workflow_id, which would then break the recreated constraint.
findings.impact: Routine rollbacks — and this repo's documented local branch-switch flow, which downgrades to a common revision — destroy user data with no warning.
findings.recommendation: Archive affected rows into a side table (or fail loudly when they exist) instead of deleting, and use `WHERE workflow_id IS NULL OR workflow_id <> ''` so no row survives to violate the constraint.

findings.title: apply_to_assistant performs the upsert and the delete in two separate transactions
findings.problem: The assistant-scope write and the workflow-row delete each open their own session with no compensation.
findings.impact: If the delete fails after the write commits, the stale workflow row keeps overriding the values the user just asked to apply everywhere — AC6 broken in a way no error message explains.
findings.recommendation: Perform both operations in one session/transaction.

findings.title: Repository scope tests are tautological
findings.problem: Both new tests assert only that the rendered SQL contains the string 'workflow_id'. Bound parameters are not rendered, so the assertions never see the value and both tests are identical — the 'defaults to the assistant scope' test verifies nothing about the default.
findings.impact: The scope predicate is described in the code as a leak-prevention invariant but is unguarded: changing the default or passing the wrong variable keeps the tests green.
findings.recommendation: Assert the bound parameters (query.compile().params) or exercise the repository against a real in-memory session.

rationale: Three lenses ran (blind, edge-case, acceptance); none failed. Nine blocking findings survive triage: CR-001 is a genuine correctness defect I introduced (two resolution paths disagree, AC12 fails), CR-002 needs a product decision about what clearing a slot means at workflow scope, CR-003/004/005 are frontend defects that undermine AC2/AC8/AC16 in practice, CR-006/008/009 are contract and test-quality defects, CR-007 is a data-loss hazard on rollback that matters here because the local branch-switch flow downgrades. Three further findings were dismissed or deferred after verification: the workflow contextvar is set/reset inside a single executor entry point and LangGraph copies contexts into worker threads, so the set(None) reset is safe (dismissed); get_mappings_by_assistant/by_user lack a scope filter but have no live callers (deferred — worth a follow-up when they gain one); workflow_id is stored without validating that the caller can access that workflow, which allows unbounded self-owned rows but leaks nothing across users (deferred). Confidence is low because CR-002 is a decision_needed finding and because the migration cannot be verified by the test suite (engine globally mocked) — manual verification is still outstanding.
